At five, Bidisha stood at the door of a neighbour's party and hid behind Mummy Nazia's legs. Mummy did not push her forward. She kept a hand on Bidisha's shoulder until Bidisha looked out at the games.
At nine, the fear had moved to school. The morning of the class recital, Bidisha's stomach felt tight and her hands were cold. Mummy Nazia's first reaction was worry, so she rang the teacher and asked whether Bidisha could skip the recital. The next week, worn out by that, Mummy went the other way. "You have to go on stage. Everyone else does it. Just be brave." Bidisha went pale and said nothing all evening. Mummy saw her small face at the dinner table and felt unsure which way was right. She spoke to Nirmala, the school counsellor. "Neither pushing nor removing it seems to help," Nirmala said. "Try tiny, steady moves with kind encouragement. Perhaps first she reads one line aloud at home, then to a friend, then on the stage." Bidisha read her line to Mummy that night, and Mummy said, "I loved hearing that," and Bidisha smiled.

qa.q: What did Mummy Nazia do first on the morning of the class recital?
qa.a: She rang the teacher and asked whether Bidisha could skip the recital.

qa.q: How do Mummy Nazia's two reactions differ from the help Nirmala suggests?
qa.a: Mummy first removed the difficulty and then forced bravery, and neither helped Bidisha. Nirmala suggested tiny, steady moves with kind encouragement, from one line at home to a friend and then the stage.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling on the morning of the recital with her tight stomach and cold hands?
qa.a: She felt frightened and anxious, and her body showed it through the tight stomach and cold hands.

qa.q: What could Mummy Nazia do if Bidisha gets stuck on one of the steps?
qa.a: She can stay at the same step for a while, praise the effort, and keep the next step small, and check with Nirmala if the fear keeps going.

grounding: A child hides at a party and gentle nearness helps (3921), and a parent swings between pushing and protecting a child anxious about a recital until small steady steps are found (4192).

At sixteen, Sabina had a civics report due on Friday. On Monday she cleaned her shelf. On Tuesday she told Rajni on the phone she would begin after dinner, and did not. If she wrote it and the teacher found it ordinary, it would show she had nothing special. The report was written in one anxious night and came out thin.
At twenty-five, Sabina joined a design firm. She handed in soft-deadline tasks late, then produced polished work in the last hour. Her manager, Gurleen, noticed the pattern. She could have said, "You need to be more disciplined." Instead she sat down beside Sabina and asked, "The client mock-up was late, but it's really strong. What made this one hard to start?" Sabina looked at the table. "I keep thinking it has to be brilliant, and if it isn't, you'll all see I'm not as good as I look." Gurleen nodded. "That's helpful to know. Let's break it into a rough version by Wednesday, and I'll look at it with you before you polish." Sabina felt her shoulders loosen for the first time that week.

qa.q: What day was Sabina's civics report due at sixteen?
qa.a: It was due on Friday.

qa.q: How does Gurleen's question at the design firm connect to Sabina's delay at sixteen?
qa.a: At sixteen Sabina put off her report from fear that an ordinary result would show she had nothing special. At the firm Gurleen asked what made the task hard instead of judging her character, and that brought out the same fear.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she told Gurleen she worried people would see she was not as good as she looked?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, fearful of being judged, and a little relieved to say it aloud.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do next to support Sabina with future tasks?
qa.a: She can agree a rough draft deadline, look at it together early, and keep asking what makes a task hard.

grounding: A teen's avoidant delay to escape judgement (4056) and a manager who asks what makes the task hard instead of judging a capable employee's last-minute pattern (3193): one person over years.

In Madhuri Ma'am's class five, reading time made Avni's heart race. When she stumbled over "vegetable", she crossed her eyes, blew out her cheeks and read the rest in a squeaky voice. The class howled, and Avni bowed, though her fingers were clenched.
At the next desk, Dilnaz had discovered a joke about a burp. She told it at lunch. Nobody laughed much, so she told it again, and again, ten times in all, louder each time. "Ugh, Dilnaz, stop," groaned one boy. Another said, "That's not even funny now." Dilnaz frowned, then tried a shorter version at the water tap: she made the burp sound and pulled a face. That time two girls giggled. Dilnaz noticed which words got the laugh and which got the groan. Madhuri Ma'am overheard and hid a smile. "Timing is a big part of jokes," she said. "Groans tell you something too." Avni watched, then sat beside Dilnaz. "Can I try one?" She told a joke about a talking spoon, and the laughter this time did not come with a racing heart.

qa.q: How many times did Dilnaz tell the joke about the burp?
qa.a: She told it ten times in all.

qa.q: How is Avni's joking different from Dilnaz's joking?
qa.a: Avni used a silly voice to stay in control after stumbling over a word, with clenched fingers showing worry. Dilnaz enjoyed a bodily joke and tested it again and again, and the groans and giggles taught her timing and audience.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she bowed with clenched fingers?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, and the joke helped her keep control of the moment.

qa.q: What could Madhuri Ma'am do to help Avni and Dilnaz enjoy humour?
qa.a: She can keep giving both time to try jokes, and quietly ask Avni how reading feels, since clowning can hide worry.

grounding: Two children in one class use humour differently: a class clown covering embarrassment (3891) and a child testing a repeated bodily joke and learning from groans (5280).

At five, Trisha slid down the hallway wall ten minutes after starting her colouring. "I'm bored. Give me the phone." Mummy Sharmila handed her a bag of buttons and a plate. "See what these can do." Trisha sighed, then sorted the buttons into a pattern of flowers and sat staring proudly at it until dinner.
At fifteen, Trisha had joined Disha Ma'am's dance class. The first weeks were fun. When the group reached a tricky footwork sequence, her steps tangled and her face went hot. The next Thursday she told Mummy, "I'm quitting. It's boring now." Mummy Sharmila put her tea down. "Is it boring, or hard?" Trisha shrugged. "Some quitting is fine. If the reasons are good, I'll support you. But maybe give it a few more sessions before you decide?" Trisha groaned but agreed. Disha Ma'am broke the sequence into slow counts and had her practise in front of the mirror. Three weeks later the steps clicked into place, and Trisha grinned at herself in the glass. She stayed, and the boring part was gone.

qa.q: What did Mummy Sharmila give Trisha when she was bored at five?
qa.a: She handed her a bag of buttons and a plate.

qa.q: How does Trisha's boredom at fifteen resemble her boredom at five, and how does it differ?
qa.a: At five, her boredom turned into a pattern of button flowers once she was given time and simple materials. At fifteen, she called a hard dance sequence boring, and the same patience, with a few more sessions and slower counts, let her get past the hard part.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when her steps tangled and her face went hot?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and embarrassed, and calling the class boring hid how hard it felt.

qa.q: What could Trisha do if she still wants to quit after several more sessions?
qa.a: She can talk with Mummy and Disha Ma'am about her reasons, decide whether quitting is a wise choice, and not leave just because of discomfort.

grounding: A child's boredom turned to play with simple materials (4068) and a teen who says a dance class is boring when it is hard, until a few more sessions bring growth (5184).

At five, Avni stopped at a party door and pressed her face into Papa Yogesh's legs. Papa did not hurry her. He kept a hand on her head until she looked around at the balloons.
At fifteen, Avni stood in the corridor after class as Vishal, in front of some others, mimicked the way she had stumbled over a word in the debate. The others laughed. Her face felt hot, and she could feel her voice going high and shaky. She took a breath. "Give me a moment out. I'll be back to talk." Then she turned and walked to the end of the hall, sat on a bench and counted her breath until her hands stopped trembling. From a distance the others thought she was running away. After ten minutes she walked back to Vishal and said calmly, "That didn't feel good. Please stop." Vishal shrugged, then muttered "Sorry." That evening Avni told Papa Yogesh about it. He listened without interrupting and said he would come with her to talk to the class teacher if it happened again.

qa.q: Where did Avni go when she said she needed a break?
qa.a: She went to the end of the hall and sat on a bench.

qa.q: How is Avni's walking away at fifteen different from her hiding at five?
qa.a: At five, hiding behind Papa gave relief from what scared her. At fifteen she walked away too, but she said she needed a moment out and would be back, then did return to speak calmly, so her leaving was a pause and not just avoidance.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when her face went hot and her voice went shaky?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, with the taunt making her upset.

qa.q: What could Avni and Papa Yogesh do if Vishal mimics her again?
qa.a: They can speak to the class teacher together, and Avni can keep using her moment-out words.

grounding: A child hides behind a parent (3921) and, as a teen, walks away from a taunt with a clear promise to return, which separates a wise break from avoidance (2509).

At five, Manjula stopped at the gate of a party and tucked herself behind Papa Mridul. When people said hello she stared at her shoes. Papa did not push her. He crouched beside her and said quietly, "We can watch for a bit." After a while she took a step out.
At fifteen, Manjula noticed her cheeks going pink whenever Tanvir walked into the room. She teased him about his shoes, then looked away. She wrote to him, then deleted it, then wrote a short message asking about the science homework. Sometimes she avoided the corridor where his locker was. Tanvir was not sure what to make of it. One day he said gently, "I like talking to you. Would you want to walk to the shop after school? It's fine if not." Manjula's heart thumped. She said, "Not this week. Maybe another time?" Tanvir nodded. "Okay, no problem." Relief and a small disappointment mixed in her chest. That evening she told Papa Mridul about it at dinner, and he smiled and said she could always tell him if anyone ever pressured her.

qa.q: What did Tanvir suggest that he and Manjula do after school?
qa.a: He asked if she would like to walk to the shop after school.

qa.q: How is Manjula's behaviour around Tanvir at fifteen like her hiding at five, and how is the response different?
qa.a: At five Manjula stared at her shoes and hid behind Papa Mridul; at fifteen her cheeks went pink, she teased Tanvir about his shoes and avoided the corridor. Papa gave gentle nearness, and Tanvir asked if she would like to walk to the shop, said it was fine if not, and accepted her answer.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she said "Not this week. Maybe another time?"
qa.a: She felt nervous and shy, with relief and a small disappointment mixed in.

qa.q: What could Manjula do next if she wants to spend time with Tanvir?
qa.a: She can send a simple message when she feels ready, and keep talking with Papa Mridul or a trusted adult if she ever feels pressured.

grounding: A child hiding at a party (3921) and a teen's first attraction shown through blushing, teasing and avoidance, met with respect and acceptance of a no (2555).
